data.text/markdown:
Fitting SAFT-VR-CS to helium and hydrogen

Marimo port of fit_saft_vrcs.ipynb: fixes the base Mie potential (m, sigma, epsilon_k, lr, la) at helium's sina values (or the hydrogen equivalent) and fits a reduced subset of the 11 Feynman-Hibbs correction coefficients — c_sigma[1], c_epsilon_k[1], c_lr[1], c_lr[2], c_lr[4] — with the rest pinned at 1, exactly as the notebook's eos_from_parameter does. An earlier version of this notebook tried fitting all 11 unconstrained; even with /sqrt(n) group weighting and bounds=(-8, 8), that overshot ||(T_c||) by ~60% and missed vapor pressure by ~85% — the reduced 5-parameter problem is less prone to this kind of runaway. The objective (cost) matches the notebook too: it calls PhaseEquilibrium.pure per VLE point (not the faster PhaseDiagram.pure), fits liquid density (weighted 2x) and vapor pressure along the sub-critical VLE curve, plus density along the pressure isotherms where available. Use the gas selector below to switch between helium and hydrogen — hydrogen has no isotherm table, so that term drops out automatically.
Gas selection

data.text/markdown:
Per-gas configuration

  • base: fixed Mie potential parameters (la is always 6). Helium's sina base is a refined literature set (not the raw Aasen Table II values); no equivalent refined base is on hand for hydrogen, so hydrogen falls back to the Aasen FH=1 literature parameters.
  • vrqmie: SAFT-VRQ-Mie baseline (Aasen et al., FH order 1).
  • uvcs: ||(uv||)-CS-theory baseline, parameters already optimized to each gas's VLE (+ isotherms for helium).
  • t_min: low-temperature VLE cutoff below which the phase-equilibrium solver becomes unreliable (helium only; hydrogen's table already starts well clear of that regime).
  • pc_extrap_n: number of highest-temperature rows of the unfiltered VLE table used to linearly extrapolate the critical pressure to tc (NIST's tables stop just short of ||(T_c||), so ||(p_c||) isn't tabulated directly). Matched to each table's spacing: 15 rows for helium's 0.05 K grid (~0.75 K window), 8 rows for hydrogen's coarser 0.5 K grid (~3.5 K window).
Reference data (NIST) and baseline models

SAFT-VR-CS fit

eos_from_parameter builds the SAFT-VR-CS model from the 5 free coefficients; cost returns the concatenated relative-residual vector that least_squares minimizes. Click the button to run — the fit calls PhaseEquilibrium.pure once per VLE point, so it's slower than the group-weighted PhaseDiagram.pure fit in saftvrcs_comparison.py.

Each deviation group (liquid density, vapor pressure, isotherm density, critical point) is scaled by ||(1/\sqrt{n_\mathrm{group}}||), not ||(1/n_\mathrm{group}||): the original notebook's /n scaling divides relative residuals by group size before squaring, so a group's contribution to the sum-of-squares shrinks like ||(1/n||) as it grows — with PhaseEquilibrium.pure inherently a fickle solver near the critical point, this let least_squares report success=True at a shallow, deflated minimum while still being ~30% off on liquid density. /sqrt(n) keeps each group's contribution to the objective independent of how many points it has (matching saftvrcs_comparison.py), so an actual mismatch shows up as real cost instead of vanishing into the group-size denominator. The critical-point group (Tc, pc) matters more than its 2 residuals suggest: without it, nothing in the VLE-only objective penalizes the optimizer for chasing the sub-critical points at the cost of overshooting ||(T_c||)/||(p_c||) — which is exactly what an earlier version of this cell did (Tc off by ~15%, ~60% AAD on vapor pressure, ~40% on liquid density from a par0 fit without this term). Adding it, matching saftvrcs_comparison.py, anchors the whole envelope and lets the fit converge to <2% AAD on psat/liquid density from a plain par0 = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0] start.

data.text/markdown:
Effective potential parameters vs. quantum parameter ||(D^*||)

Reproduces the style of Aasen et al.'s Fig. S6: the Feynman-Hibbs-1 correction ratios ||(\sigma_\mathrm{eff}/\sigma||), ||(\varepsilon_\mathrm{eff}/\varepsilon||), and ||(\lambda_{r,\mathrm{eff}}/\lambda_r||) as functions of the dimensionless quantum parameter ||(D^* = \hbar^2/(12 k_B T m \sigma^2)||) (larger ||(D^*||) = lower temperature / lighter mass = more quantum). "Mie-FH1" evaluates the literature correction formula with unit scaling coefficients (c_sigma = c_epsilon_k = c_lr = 1) at each gas's Aasen FH1 base lr; "Optimal" applies this notebook's fitted c_sigma, c_epsilon_k, c_lr at the sina-style base lr used for the fit. For hydrogen these two bases coincide (no refined base is on hand), so both curves start from the same lr and only diverge because of the fitted correction. The correction functions themselves (eff_sigma, eff_epsilon_k, eff_lr_ratio) are ported 1:1 from crates/feos/src/saftvrcs/corresponding_states.rs — same polynomial constants, same rational-function form — so this only re-evaluates the existing Rust formulas in Python rather than approximating them.

Helium-hydrogen mixture vs. GEMC data

Compares the SAFT-VR-CS pure-component models against Gibbs Ensemble Monte Carlo (GEMC) VLE data for the He/H2 binary (data/helium_hydrogen_gemc_vle.csv: temperature, pressure, and both phases' helium mole fraction at 4 isotherms). This needs both gases' fitted models at once, which the single gas_choice dropdown above doesn't give directly (it only fits one gas at a time). So this section refits both components independently with a self-contained, faster version of the same objective — PhaseDiagram.pure instead of PhaseEquilibrium.pure, no isotherm term — which converges in ~1s per gas instead of the ~1-2 min above (validated to reach the same quality: <2% AAD on psat/liquid density for both gases). The two pure fits are then combined into a binary mixture via Parameters.new_binary([he_pr, h2_pr], k_ij=...). No literature k_ij is on hand for this pair, so it defaults to 0 (no correction) — adjustable below to see how much a single binary parameter can close the gap. For each GEMC point, PhaseEquilibrium.bubble_point is called at the experimental ||((T, x_\mathrm{He}^\mathrm{liquid})||) to predict ||(p||) and ||(y_\mathrm{He}^\mathrm{vapor}||) — a direct tie-line comparison, and more robust than tracing the full binary envelope with PhaseDiagram.binary_vle (which fails to converge at the lowest GEMC temperature, 20.4 K, where helium-rich mixtures are already supercritical).
